candidates.note: This ribbed copper-alloy bucket is one of two Italian vessels in the Hassle hoard, discovered in Sweden in 1936. The museum dates the vessel to 550–500 BCE. Its northern Italian production origin is separate from the Swedish findspot; this record represents one bucket rather than the whole hoard.
candidates.source_description:
This [Etruscan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Etruscan_civilization) bucket, a so-called "Ciste a cordoni" has probably been used to serve beer or mead here in Scandinavia. Originally in Italy it was probably wine in the bucket. It is made from hammered copper alloy and has a rich decor. The bucket is part of one the most fascinating [treasures](https://bit.ly/3su35wG) in the collections of the Swedish History Museum and was found in [Hassle](https://bit.ly/3JZps32<), Glanshammar parish in northeastern Närke. Sometime around 500 BC a large cauldron from the eastern Mediterranean, two buckets from northern Italy and two swords and 12 horse ornaments from Central Europe was sacrificed in a fen.

Online Collections: [96979_HST](https://bit.ly/3MdcPn8)

candidates.geography: Etruria, central Italy (production region; exact workshop unknown)
candidates.original_location: Etruria, central Italy (production region; exact workshop unknown)
candidates.subject: Etruscan pottery, bronze vessels, funerary art and architectural sculpture
candidates.year: 5th century BCE (museum tour; formal record: 1st millennium BCE)
candidates.object_identity: The Hunt Museum; MG 015
candidates.scan_source: Physical-object scan published by its holding institution or documented archaeological digitization partner
candidates.attribution: 3D model “Schnabelkanne, beak-spouted flagon” by The Hunt Museum (TheHuntMuseum), via Sketchfab, CC0 1.0. Atrium may serve an optimized derivative; authored source appearance must be preserved.
candidates.note: A bronze wine flagon with a beaked spout, a splayed foot and a separately cast handle ending in animal heads. It is the original museum vessel, distinct from the enlarged modern sculpture made from its scan for the museum garden. The museum guide dates it to the 5th century BCE; the formal collection record gives the broader 1st millennium BCE.
candidates.source_description: Culture: [Etruscan](http://vocab.getty.edu/page/aat/300020471) Material: Bronze  Dims: H 25.9 Accession No: MG 015 Current Location: [The Hunt Museum](https://www.huntmuseum.com/), [Limerick](https://www.geonames.org/7778675/limerick-city.html). A beak-spouted flagon of beaten bronze on a splayed base with a bulbous shoulder, narrow neck and flat rimmed pouring mouth. The [cast](http://vocab.getty.edu/page/aat/300053104) handle has a terminal on the body, decorated with a palmette, S-spirals and scrolls ending in a lotus flower above and a lyre below. Above, the handle forks ending in two animal heads with setback ears appearing to represent crouching felines. This is a type known as ‘Schnabelkanne’, a distinctly ['Celtic'](http://vocab.getty.edu/page/aat/300019470) style manufactured from the late sixth-century BC in Etruria. They were often placed in Celtic princely graves and traces of wine have been found in some flagons. [More](https://tinyurl.com/bd4sef73).

candidates.source_description:
Etruscan kylix from the Necropolis of Poggio Pinci, Asciano, Tuscany, Italy

Etruscan kylix with two horizontal handles. Yellow-beige clay with black paint. Decorated disk on interior center, with reddish painted over: male figure and geometric elements. Product of the Sokra group with parallels from Tarquinia. Second half of the 4th c. BCE. Tomb II.127, Necropolis of Poggio Pinci, Asciano. Mangani 1983, n. cat. II, 3. Displayed at the Civic Museum of Archaeology and Sacred Art at Palazzo Corboli, Asciano.   

Processed in Reality Capture from 508 images. GDH ID No. C2_127 

This project was done under the authority of the Soprintendenza Archeologia, belle arti e paesaggio per le province di Siena Grosseto e Arezzo in collaboration with Global Digital Heritage and the Municipality of Asciano. We thank Elisa, Benedetta and all the staff from Palazzo Corboli for making the collection accessible and our work easier.
